even_node_count.what: This cluster runs an even number of nodes, so a network partition can split it into two equal halves with no majority — quorum queues then can't elect a leader and may stall. Run an odd node count so a majority always survives.
even_node_count.fixTitle: Move to an odd node count
fixSteps: Add or remove one node so the total is odd (3, 5, …).
Spread quorum-queue replicas across the surviving majority.
Re-scan to confirm the finding clears.

version_skew.what: Nodes in this cluster run different RabbitMQ versions. Mixed versions are only meant to exist briefly during an upgrade — left in place they risk behaviour drift and block quorum/Khepri operations.
fixSteps: Plan a rolling upgrade so every node lands on the same minor version.
Upgrade lagging nodes one at a time, checking cluster health between each.
Re-scan once all nodes report the same version.

prefetch_misconfig.what: Consumers on {{resource}} use a prefetch (QoS) setting likely to hurt throughput or fairness — unbounded prefetch lets one consumer hoard messages, while a prefetch of 1 serialises work and adds round-trips.
fixSteps: Set a bounded channel prefetch (start around 20–100 and measure).
Make sure every consumer acks so prefetch credit is returned.
Re-scan after redeploying the consumers.

orphan.what: Exchange {{resource}} has no bindings, so anything published to it is silently dropped (or returned if mandatory). It's usually a leftover from a renamed route or a deleted queue.
fixSteps: Confirm whether any publisher still targets this exchange.
If it's needed, bind it to the queue(s) it should route to.
If it's truly orphaned, delete it, then re-scan.

fd_limit_low.what: A node's file-descriptor limit is low relative to its connection and queue count. RabbitMQ uses one FD per connection and several per queue — running near the limit causes accept() failures and dropped connections under load.
fixSteps: Raise the OS ulimit (and systemd LimitNOFILE) for the broker process.
Aim for headroom well above peak connections × ~1.5.
Restart the node and re-scan.

watermark_misconfig.what: The memory high-watermark on {{resource}} is set high enough that, under load, the broker can hit the alarm and block all publishers cluster-wide before you have room to react.
fixSteps: Review per-node memory headroom first.
Lower vm_memory_high_watermark (e.g. to 0.6) on the affected nodes.
Watch the alarm state after applying, then re-scan.

conflicting.what: Two policies match {{resource}} at the same priority, and RabbitMQ applies only one — the winner is non-deterministic at equal priority, so your queues may silently get the wrong settings.
fixSteps: Decide which definitions {{resource}} actually needs.
Merge them, narrow the patterns so they don't overlap, or re-prioritise so the intended one wins.
Re-scan to confirm only one policy applies.

classic_mirrored_deprecated.what: {{resource}} is a classic mirrored queue. Classic mirroring is deprecated and removed in RabbitMQ 4.x — quorum queues are the supported replacement for replicated durability.
fixSteps: Create a new quorum queue alongside the classic one (it can't be converted in place).
Drain consumers, cut publishers over, then retire the old queue.
Re-scan once the classic queue is gone.

exclusive_in_production.what: {{resource}} is an exclusive queue — it's deleted the moment its declaring connection drops. That's fine for RPC reply queues but dangerous for anything that must survive a reconnect.
fixSteps: Confirm the queue is genuinely tied to one short-lived connection.
If the data must outlive the connection, redeclare it durable and non-exclusive.
Re-scan after the change.

missing_dlx.what: {{resource}} has no dead-letter exchange, so rejected (requeue=false) or TTL-expired messages are dropped silently with no audit trail — you can't inspect or replay failures.
fixSteps: Create a dead-letter exchange and a queue bound to it that you control.
Apply x-dead-letter-exchange via policy or queue argument on {{resource}}.
Re-scan to confirm the finding clears.

no_consumer_backlog.what: {{resource}} has no protection against an unbounded backlog — with no length limit, TTL, or overflow handling, a stalled consumer lets messages pile up until memory or disk alarms fire.
fixSteps: Set a max-length or message-TTL appropriate to the workload.
Choose an overflow behaviour (drop-head or reject-publish) deliberately.
Re-scan after applying the policy.

no_length_bound.what: {{resource}} has neither a max-length nor a message-TTL, so it can grow without bound if producers outpace consumers — eventually triggering memory or disk alarms that block the whole node.
no_length_bound.fixTitle: Add a length or TTL bound
fixSteps: Decide the right ceiling (max-length, max-length-bytes, or message-TTL).
Apply it via a policy so it's easy to tune later.
Re-scan to confirm the bound is in place.

quorum_queue_ha_policy.what: {{resource}} is a quorum queue but a classic HA (ha-mode) policy still matches it. HA policies are meaningless for quorum queues and signal a half-finished migration off classic mirroring.
fixSteps: Narrow or remove the ha-mode policy so it no longer matches quorum queues.
Confirm replication is governed by the quorum queue's own replica settings.
Re-scan to confirm the stale policy is gone.

quorum_queue_minority_replicas.what: {{resource}} has its quorum-queue replicas placed so that a single node failure loses the majority — the queue then becomes unavailable until the node returns.
fixSteps: Grow the replica set to an odd number spread across distinct nodes.
Use rabbitmq-queues add_member / grow to rebalance.
Re-scan to confirm a majority survives one node loss.

quorum_queue_no_delivery_limit.what: {{resource}} is a quorum queue with no delivery-limit, so a poison message can be redelivered forever — looping through consumers without ever being dead-lettered.
fixSteps: Set x-delivery-limit (via policy) to a sensible retry count.
Pair it with a dead-letter exchange so exhausted messages are captured.
Re-scan after applying.

transient_in_production.what: {{resource}} is a transient (non-durable) queue — it's lost on broker restart along with its messages. That's rarely what you want for a production workload.
fixSteps: Confirm the queue's data should survive a restart.
Redeclare it durable (transient/durable can't be toggled in place).
Re-scan after the change.

guest_enabled.what: The default guest user is still enabled. Even limited to localhost by default, leaving it active is a well-known weak spot and fails most hardening checks.
guest_enabled.fixTitle: Disable or replace the guest user
fixSteps: Create named users with least-privilege permissions for each app.
Delete the guest user (or at minimum change its password and restrict it).
Re-scan to confirm guest is gone.

default_unscoped.what: Production traffic is running on the default vhost ("/"). A single shared vhost gives no isolation boundary for permissions, policies, or limits between apps.
fixSteps: Create a vhost per app or environment.
Move queues/exchanges and grant scoped permissions there.
Re-scan once the default vhost no longer carries production traffic.
